desc:
A rotation of a string moves some number of characters from the front to the back: rotating "abcde" by two gives "cdeab". Among all n rotations of s (including the unrotated string), return the one that is smallest in dictionary order.

For example, the rotations of "bca" are "bca", "cab" and "abc", so the answer is "abc". For "cbaab" the answer is "aabcb".
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Generating all rotations and taking the minimum costs O(n²) time (and memory if you store them). Think about how to compare two rotations without building them.

Two candidate start positions i and j can be compared character by character using indices modulo n. If they agree for k characters and then s[i+k] > s[j+k], then none of the starts i, i+1, ..., i+k can be the best.

Keep two candidates and a match length k. On a difference, the larger candidate jumps by k + 1; if the candidates collide, move one forward. Stop when one candidate or k reaches n; the answer starts at the smaller candidate.
editorial: The two-candidate method (a form of Booth's / Duval-style minimal representation) works in linear time. Hold two start indices i = 0, j = 1 and a counter k of characters that already agree. Compare s[(i+k) % n] with s[(j+k) % n].

If they are equal, increase k. If the character at i is larger, then every start i, i+1, ..., i+k is beaten by the corresponding start shifted by j - i, so set i += k + 1; symmetrically for j. After a jump, if the two candidates coincide push j forward by one, and reset k = 0.

Each step advances at least one of i or j (or k towards n), and both candidates stay below n, so the loop makes O(n) iterations. When it ends, min(i, j) is the starting index of the smallest rotation (when k reaches n the string is periodic and both candidates give the same rotation). Return s[start:] + s[:start].
